clue.text: One swimming here suffers from exposure

definitions.text: One swimming here suffers from exposure

parts.words: One swimming here suffers from exposure
parts.note: reads like a cold swimmer at risk of hypothermia, but means a pet fish in a clear glass container, on view to everyone in the room

explanation.surface: A warning that open-water swimmers risk exposure to the cold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exposure' suggests chill and hypothermia; here it means being constantly on show, the lot of a pet fish behind clear glass.
explanation.definitionFit: A round glass container for a pet fish leaves it permanently on display, hence the idiom for a life without privacy.

clue.text: School's good press hard to repeat in turn

parts.note: to ram is to press or force hard

indicators.note: the instruction to repeat the previous piece, turned round, so the same word is written a second time backwards

parts.note: the same verb meaning to force hard, used again

explanation.surface: A school prides itself on a good press, which it must keep repeating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to repeat in turn' gives RAM again, reversed to MAR. The 's on School stands for 'is', joining definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A grammar school is a selective British secondary school, so the word alone can stand for that kind of school.

clue.text: Aliens seen crossing the road?

parts.note: the small illuminated figure on a pedestrian crossing signal, which tells walkers they may cross, recast as visiting extraterrestrials

explanation.surface: A tabloid query about extraterrestrials spotted walking across a street.
explanation.walkthrough: At British pedestrian crossings a lit green figure shows when it is safe to walk; the clue pictures those tiny figures as the stock science-fiction visitors from Mars.
explanation.definitionFit: The stock cartoon image of extraterrestrials is of small green humanoids, a jokey phrase for space visitors.

clue.text: Strength of front in which temperature drops

indicators.note: says the temperature letter goes within the word for front, which holds it

parts.note: fore means the front part, as in the fore of a ship
T, the abbreviation for temperature, is the letter that drops into place here

explanation.surface: A weather report about the strength of a cold front as temperatures fall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Front' and 'temperature drops' look like meteorology; 'in which' places T within FORE, the temperature letter dropping into it.
explanation.definitionFit: A person's strong point or special talent is their forte, from the Italian for strong.

clue.text: One luxurious edition of bestiary

indicators.note: a new edition reworks the text, so the letters of the following word appear in a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A lavish printing of a medieval book of beasts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One luxurious edition' reads as a single fine copy, but 'One luxurious' is the definition and 'edition of' rearranges BESTIARY.
explanation.definitionFit: A sybarite is a lover of luxury and sensual pleasure, after the famously self-indulgent people of ancient Sybaris.

clue.text: I hear he starts game, a sort of test

indicators.note: signals that the word must be said out loud and matched to another of the same sound

parts.note: a beater on a shoot is the man who drives game birds out of cover so they rise

explanation.surface: Someone has been told that a man begins a game, which is some kind of test.
explanation.walkthrough: 'starts game' means flushes birds or animals into the open, not kicking off a match. In a non-rhotic British accent BEATER and BETA sound alike.
explanation.definitionFit: Software goes through a beta test, the trial release to outside users before launch.

clue.text: Wine lover is dreadful glutton

indicators.note: something dreadful is in a bad way, so the letters are mangled into a new order

explanation.surface: A wine buff is condemned as a greedy guzzler.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is' links. 'Glutton' is a person in the surface but the definition is an animal.
explanation.definitionFit: The wolverine, a large northern weasel known for its voracious appetite, is also called the glutton.

clue.text: Tie-break system to end argument

parts.note: a goal is an end or aim
a difference is a disagreement or argument, as in 'settle our differences'

explanation.surface: A procedure for breaking a deadlock so that a dispute can be ended.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to' is a link. In football league tables, teams level on points are separated by goals scored minus goals conceded.
explanation.definitionFit: In league football, teams equal on points are separated by goals scored minus conceded, a standard tie-break.

clue.text: Formal quality displayed by best architecture

indicators.note: the letters are on show inside the following words, running across the gap between them

explanation.surface: Formality is on show in the finest buildings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'displayed by' finds the run spanning the end of 'best' and the start of 'architecture'.
explanation.definitionFit: Starch figuratively means stiffness or formality of manner, as in a starchy person.

clue.text: It grows more quickly if pruned

indicators.note: pruning cuts something back, here lopping the first letter off the word

parts.note: faster means more quickly

explanation.surface: Gardening advice that a plant flourishes when cut back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'if pruned' takes the F off the front of FASTER. The surface sounds like horticultural truth, which suits a flower.
explanation.definitionFit: An aster is a daisy-like garden flower, so it is something that grows.

clue.text: Drunk often has to withdraw feebly

definitions.meaning: a drinker usually has a bottle on the go, brought out ready to pour
to lose one's nerve and pull out of something, British slang

explanation.surface: A heavy drinker is often forced into a weak retreat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to' links the two. To bottle out is British slang for losing your nerve; 'bottle' means courage.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang uses bottle for courage, so losing it and pulling back from a challenge is the phrase.

clue.text: Harbour children go round in the cold

definitions.meaning: the prefabricated floating harbours towed to Normandy for the D-Day landings bore this code name

definitions.text: children go round in the cold
definitions.meaning: the nursery rhyme in which children circle a bush on a cold and frosty morning

explanation.surface: Children in a port play a ring game in winter.
explanation.walkthrough: The nursery rhyme 'Here We Go Round the ___ Bush' has the line 'on a cold and frosty morning'; the D-Day temporary harbours shared the name.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses name the same tree word: the WWII artificial harbour and the bush of the playground song.

clue.text: Bank clerk who worked on the hydrogen bomb.

definitions.meaning: a cashier who counts money at a bank counter

definitions.text: who worked on the hydrogen bomb.
definitions.meaning: Edward, the Hungarian-American physicist called the father of the H-bomb

explanation.surface: A bank cashier with a secret past in nuclear weapons research.
explanation.walkthrough: Two senses: a bank cashier, and the surname of the physicist central to the US hydrogen bomb project.
explanation.definitionFit: A bank cashier counts out money, an old sense of tell meaning to count.

clue.text: Control English army pistol's recoil

indicators.note: a gun's recoil kicks it backwards, so the whole string of pieces runs in reverse

parts.note: TA is the Territorial Army, Britain's reserve force
the Luger is a German semi-automatic pistol; the 's is possessive

explanation.surface: Someone must control the kickback from a British soldier's handgun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recoil' turns E + TA + LUGER, giving REGUL AT E. TA, the Territorial Army, is Britain's volunteer reserve.
explanation.definitionFit: To regulate is to control or govern something, keeping it within rules.

clue.text: Exciting parcel, and she barely moves close

indicators.note: exciting stirs things up, so the letters are thoroughly mixed

explanation.surface: An erotic parcel arrives, and a nearly naked woman sidles up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exciting' rearranges PARCEL AND. 'barely' means scantily dressed, and 'close' means near a customer.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman who dances provocatively, nearly naked, right on or by a seated customer in a club fits the description.

clue.text: Fairly good treatment, on the surface

definitions.meaning: jokily read as 'fine-ish', meaning reasonably fine
the final coat of varnish, polish or texture given to a surface

explanation.surface: A review saying a product's surface coating is passable.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is a pun: fine plus the suffix -ish, meaning fairly fine.
explanation.definitionFit: A surface treatment such as varnish or polish is called a finish; fairly good is read as fine-ish.

clue.text: Porter brought in cut of meat to one ill with this?

indicators.note: the meat is brought into the drink, so it sits inside that word

parts.note: porter is a dark beer
a rib is a cut of meat
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A hospital porter carries a joint of meat to a patient, who is perhaps ill as a result.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Porter' is the dark beer, not a hospital worker; 'brought in' signals the container. The definition leans on the whole clue: one ill with this disease.
explanation.definitionFit: Beriberi is a disease of vitamin B1 deficiency, the illness a sufferer might have.

clue.text: Monumental builder cuts round back of stone

indicators.note: the word for cuts goes round the other letter, enclosing it

parts.note: chops means cuts with blows

indicators.note: the back of a word is its last letter

explanation.surface: A mason shaping blocks trims around the rear of a stone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back of stone' is E, and 'round' wraps CHOPS around it.
explanation.definitionFit: The pharaoh Cheops (Khufu) built the Great Pyramid of Giza, the most monumental of all buildings.

clue.text: Squeezes regiment at first into quarters

indicators.note: the first piece goes into the word for quarters

parts.note: camps are quarters, places where troops are lodged

indicators.note: takes the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: An army unit is crammed into its billets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at first' gives R from regiment; 'into' puts it inside CAMPS.
explanation.definitionFit: To cramp is to confine or squeeze into too little space.

clue.text: Never many after 3 in plant

indicators.note: puts the always-few phrase after the letter from clue 3

parts.note: the answer to clue 3, Strength, is the musical direction for loud, written f in a score
never many means always few

explanation.surface: A gardener says not much grows after the third plot.
explanation.walkthrough: '3' sends you to 3-down, whose musical abbreviation is F. 'Never many' rephrases as 'ever few'.
explanation.definitionFit: Feverfew is a daisy-like herb, traditionally taken against fevers and headaches.

clue.text: Decline to admit veto overturned but hopeful

indicators.note: the word for decline lets the other in, holding it inside

parts.note: to wane is to decline

indicators.note: the veto is overturned, turned over so its letters run backwards

parts.note: a ban is a veto

explanation.surface: Someone refuses to accept that their veto was overruled but stays optimistic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'overturned' reverses the veto word and 'to admit' sets it inside the decline word; 'but' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A wannabe is an aspiring hopeful who wants to be someone or something.

clue.text: Make tough girl walk on the inside

parts.note: Anne is a girl's name

indicators.note: the inside of a word is all but its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A girl is told to toughen up by taking a stroll indoors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the inside' of walk is AL; 'on' links the two parts.
explanation.definitionFit: Annealing metal or glass by heating and slow cooling makes it tougher and less brittle.

clue.text: End of cigarette burning, join the traffic

parts.note: a filter is the tip at the end of a cigarette
a fire that is in is still burning

explanation.surface: A driver flicks a cigarette end, still alight, and joins the traffic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'End of cigarette' looks like a selection of its last letter but means the filter tip.
explanation.definitionFit: Drivers filter in when they merge into a stream of traffic from a side lane.

clue.text: Add a little reason why pregnant seal comes ashore

definitions.meaning: to replenish by adding a small amount, as with a drink

definitions.text: reason why pregnant seal comes ashore
definitions.meaning: seals haul out on land to give birth to young, read as two words

explanation.surface: Seals giving birth on beaches add a little to the population.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is read as 'to pup', a seal coming ashore to give birth.
explanation.definitionFit: To refill a glass or tank partly, adding a little more, is a common phrase for replenishing.

clue.text: Communicate to the deaf, and add name

definitions.meaning: to use hand gestures in ... language
to write one's signature on a document

explanation.surface: Someone uses sign language and adds a signature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'and' links two senses of the same verb.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb covers both using sign language and putting your signature to something.

clue.text: Rep's arranged drug on bed, as doctor may order

indicators.note: in an across clue, on means placed after the preceding pieces
arranged puts the letters into a fresh order

parts.note: the letters of rep and its s
a crib is a child's bed
E is ecstasy

explanation.surface: A sales rep has set up a drug to accompany bed rest, as a GP might.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arranged' scrambles the rep letters; 'on' places the drug after the bed in this across clue. E for ecstasy is a crossword staple.
explanation.definitionFit: Prescribing is what a doctor does when ordering a medicine or treatment for a patient.

clue.text: Creature slept briefly (an hour less) in retirement

indicators.note: retiring means going backwards, so the remaining letters are read in reverse
take away the letter for hour

parts.note: had a nap means slept briefly

explanation.surface: An animal dozed for a short while, an hour short, after retiring to bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'less' removes H to leave ADNAP, and 'in retirement' turns it around. 'an' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The giant panda is a black-and-white bear, a creature in the plainest sense.

clue.text: Illustration is perfection, once fixed

indicators.note: something fixed or rigged has been tampered with, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A picture is perfect once it has been framed and mounted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'once fixed' rearranges IS PERFECTION.
explanation.definitionFit: A frontispiece is an illustration facing a book's title page.
